title: Degenerative Musculoskeletal Diseases
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers degenerative diseases of cartilage, bone, disc, and fascia: osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, Paget disease of bone, and avascular necrosis, followed by the age-specific hip and knee disorders of childhood and adolescence, intervertebral disc disease, and Dupuytren contracture. Each is a failure of tissue maintenance. Cartilage matrix breaks down faster than chondrocytes rebuild it, osteoclasts outpace osteoblasts, remodeling becomes chaotic, or a region with little collateral flow loses its blood supply. Board questions usually give the patient's age, the joint or bone involved, and a lab or imaging clue, then ask for the mechanism. Knowing which cell, matrix, or vessel fails in each disease lets you predict the findings instead of memorizing them.

blocks.text: Articular cartilage is avascular and aneural hyaline cartilage nourished by synovial fluid. Its type II collagen network restrains aggrecan, whose chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains carry fixed negative charges that draw in water. Under load, water is squeezed out and the swollen matrix pushes back; when the load lifts, water returns. This lets cartilage spread force across the joint and keeps friction near zero. Sparse chondrocytes maintain the matrix, but slowly, because they have no blood supply and little capacity to divide.

Osteoarthritis (OA), also called degenerative joint disease, begins when mechanical stress or aging injures chondrocytes. The cells first proliferate into clusters and try to repair, then shift to a catabolic state. They release interleukin 1 beta, tumor necrosis factor, and nitric oxide, which induce matrix metalloproteinases (especially MMP-13, a collagenase) and aggrecanases (ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5). Aggrecan is lost first, so the cartilage softens; then the collagen network is cleaved and vertical clefts form, called fibrillation. Fragments break off into the joint as loose bodies (joint mice), and full-thickness loss eventually exposes bone. Aging adds chondrocyte senescence and advanced glycation end products that stiffen collagen and make it brittle.

Bone reacts once cartilage no longer cushions it. Subchondral bone thickens (sclerosis), and bone rubbing on bone is polished smooth (eburnation). Synovial fluid forced through cartilage defects and microfractures, together with focal bone necrosis, produces subchondral cysts. At the joint margins, growth factors such as TGF-beta stimulate new cartilage that ossifies by the endochondral route into osteophytes. Mild synovitis is common, but OA is not driven by systemic autoimmunity, and the joint does not fuse.

sections.title: Clinical and radiographic findings of osteoarthritis

blocks.text: Every OA finding follows from mechanical cartilage failure. Cartilage has no nerves, so pain comes from the structures around it: subchondral bone with raised intraosseous pressure and microfractures, periosteum lifted by osteophytes, an irritated synovium, and a stretched capsule and ligaments. Pain is therefore worse with use and weight bearing and eases with rest; in advanced disease it may also occur at rest and at night.

Stiffness after inactivity is brief, usually under 30 minutes, and is often called gelling. It is short because the synovium is not filled with an inflammatory exudate. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), inflammatory synovitis causes morning stiffness lasting longer than an hour. Examination shows bony enlargement, crepitus as roughened surfaces grind, reduced range of motion, and at most a small cool effusion.

The joint pattern follows load. OA involves the knees (most often the medial compartment), hips, lumbar and cervical spine, first metatarsophalangeal joint, and in the hand the distal interphalangeal (DIP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and first carpometacarpal joints. Heberden nodes at the DIP joints and Bouchard nodes at the PIP joints are osteophytes, so they are hard and bony, unlike the soft, spindle-shaped PIP swelling of RA. The metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and wrists are usually spared. Involvement is asymmetric because each joint has its own load history.

Laboratory tests are normal: erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are not raised, and rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are negative. Synovial fluid is clear and viscous with fewer than about 2,000 white cells per microliter. Radiographs show the cartilage loss indirectly as joint space narrowing that is uneven within the joint, plus osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and subchondral cysts. There is no periarticular osteopenia and no marginal erosion, because there is no inflammatory pannus. Radiographic severity correlates only loosely with pain.

blocks.text: Osteoporosis is reduced bone mass with normal mineralization. The bone that remains has a normal ratio of mineral to osteoid; there is simply less of it, with thin cortices and thin, disconnected trabeculae. This distinguishes it from osteomalacia, in which osteoid accumulates because it cannot be mineralized. Loss of architecture, not only loss of mass, lowers strength, so fractures follow minor trauma.

Adult bone is continually remodeled by basic multicellular units in which osteoclasts resorb a packet of bone and osteoblasts refill it. Bone mass at any age equals peak bone mass, reached in about the third decade, minus later losses. Peak mass is set largely by genetics, with contributions from calcium and vitamin D intake, physical activity, and sex hormones during puberty. A low peak leaves less reserve to lose. From about the fourth decade, each remodeling cycle in both sexes refills slightly less than was removed.

Estrogen loss at menopause accelerates this imbalance, with the fastest loss in the first several years. Osteoblasts, stromal cells, and osteocytes produce RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and drives their fusion, activation, and survival. Osteoprotegerin (OPG) acts as a decoy receptor that binds RANKL. Estrogen suppresses RANKL, supports OPG, limits interleukin 1, interleukin 6, and TNF production, and promotes osteoclast apoptosis. Without it, more remodeling units are activated, each resorbs more than is replaced, and trabecular bone, with the largest surface area, thins first. Age-related (senile) osteoporosis adds reduced osteoblast number and responsiveness, less physical loading, and lower calcium absorption with mild secondary hyperparathyroidism, so cortical bone is also lost. Estrogen derived from testosterone also protects male bone.

blocks.title: Postmenopausal osteoporosis
steps: Estrogen falls at menopause
RANKL rises, osteoprotegerin falls, IL-1, IL-6, TNF rise

Resorption exceeds formation in each remodeling unit
Trabecular bone thins and loses connections first
Fragility fractures of vertebrae, distal radius, then hip
blocks.caption: Estrogen loss shifts the RANKL to osteoprotegerin balance toward resorption.

blocks.text: Osteoporosis is silent until a bone breaks, and the fracture sites follow the type of bone lost. Vertebral bodies and the distal radius are rich in trabecular bone, so they fail early, often in the 50s and 60s. Vertebral compression fractures, most common in the mid thoracic spine and at the thoracolumbar junction, collapse the anterior body into a wedge; many are painless and are discovered as height loss or as thoracic kyphosis (dowager hump). A fall on an outstretched hand breaks the distal radius (Colles fracture). Hip fractures of the femoral neck or intertrochanteric region involve both cortical and trabecular bone, occur later, usually after a fall, and carry the greatest morbidity and mortality.

Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and PTH are normal. Mineral regulation is intact, and the slow imbalance in remodeling draws on a skeletal calcium reserve far larger than the extracellular pool, so homeostasis holds plasma values steady. ALP may rise briefly while a fracture heals. Abnormal values point to another diagnosis or a secondary cause, as the table shows.

blocks.title: Serum findings in diseases that lower bone density
blocks.caption: Approximate adult reference ranges: total calcium about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL, phosphate about 2.5 to 4.5 mg/dL, ALP about 40 to 130 U/L (higher in growing adolescents; varies by laboratory).

blocks.text: Plain radiographs detect reduced density only after roughly 30% or more of bone mass is lost, so dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) is used to measure bone mineral density at the lumbar spine, total hip, and femoral neck. The T-score compares the patient with the mean of healthy young adults of the same sex, in standard deviations. A Z-score compares the patient with people of the same age and sex and is used for children, premenopausal women, and younger men, in whom a low value suggests a secondary cause.

blocks.title: WHO categories by DEXA T-score
rows: Minus 2.5 or lower plus a fragility fracture
blocks.caption: A hip or vertebral fragility fracture establishes clinical osteoporosis regardless of the T-score.

blocks.title: Reading a DEXA report
blocks.text: A 70-year-old woman has T-scores of minus 2.2 at the femoral neck and minus 1.4 at L1 to L4, with normal calcium, phosphate, and ALP. Step 1: classify by the lowest valid site, here the femoral neck, so she has osteopenia. Step 2: question the spine value. Osteophytes, facet sclerosis, and aortic calcification from age-related degeneration add mineral to the spine measurement and falsely raise it, so the hip is more reliable in older adults. Step 3: if her lateral spine film shows a wedge compression fracture after minimal trauma, the diagnosis becomes osteoporosis despite a T-score above minus 2.5. Step 4: normal labs fit primary osteoporosis; a high ALP would redirect you to osteomalacia or Paget disease.

blocks.predict: Why are serum calcium and ALP normal in a woman who has lost a third of her trabecular bone?
blocks.explain: The mineral that remains is normal, PTH and vitamin D regulation are intact, and the slow net loss is buffered by a large skeletal reserve; ALP reflects osteoblast activity, which is not increased.

sections.title: Paget disease of bone: mechanism and laboratory findings

blocks.text: Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is a localized disorder of remodeling in which excessive osteoclast activity is followed by rapid, disorganized osteoblastic repair. It affects adults, usually over 55 and rarely before 40, is more common in people of northern European descent, and most often involves the pelvis, spine, skull, femur, and tibia. Most patients have several bones involved (polyostotic). Many are asymptomatic and are found because of a raised ALP or an incidental radiograph.

The primary abnormality is in the osteoclast. Pagetic osteoclasts are enlarged, carry many more nuclei than normal (up to about 100), and are hyperresponsive to RANKL and vitamin D. Mutations in SQSTM1, which encodes p62, a scaffold protein in the RANK to NF-kappa B pathway, occur in many familial and some sporadic cases and increase osteoclast signaling. A slow paramyxovirus infection of osteoclasts has been proposed but is not proven.

blocks.title: Phases of Paget disease
steps: Lytic phase: giant osteoclasts resorb bone
Marrow replaced by loose, highly vascular fibrous tissue
Mixed phase: osteoblasts rapidly lay down woven bone
Woven bone remodeled into irregular lamellar bone
Sclerotic phase: thick, dense, disorganized bone
Burned-out phase: quiescent mosaic lamellar bone
blocks.caption: Phases can coexist in different bones or regions of one bone.

blocks.text: Because resorption and formation repeat in short, random cycles, the final bone is lamellar bone crossed by irregular cement lines in a jigsaw or mosaic pattern. It is thicker and larger than normal but its collagen is not aligned along lines of stress, so it bends and breaks under loads normal bone tolerates. On imaging, the lytic front in a long bone advances as a sharp, flame-shaped edge, the skull shows a well-defined lytic area (osteoporosis circumscripta) and later a patchy cotton wool appearance, and affected bones show coarse trabeculae, cortical thickening, and enlargement. Radionuclide bone scans show intense uptake.

Laboratory findings reflect high turnover with balanced mineral handling. Serum ALP, a marker of osteoblast activity, is raised, often markedly, while calcium, phosphate, and PTH are normal because resorption and formation remain coupled. Resorption markers such as urinary hydroxyproline and N-telopeptide are also raised. Hypercalcemia appears mainly when a patient is immobilized, because formation then falls while resorption continues.

Each complication of Paget disease follows from three properties of pagetic bone: it is enlarged, it is mechanically weak, and it is highly vascular. Enlargement compresses neighboring nerves and narrows foramina and canals. Weakness causes bowing and fracture. Vascularity shunts blood and makes the bone feel warm. Lifelong high cell turnover increases the risk of malignant transformation.

blocks.text: High-output heart failure needs extensive disease. Blood flow through hypervascular pagetic bone and the overlying skin can rise many times above normal, and these low-resistance channels behave like arteriovenous fistulas. Total peripheral resistance falls, cardiac output must rise to maintain arterial pressure, and the volume load can exhaust an older heart, especially one already damaged by coronary or valve disease.

Osteosarcoma normally peaks in adolescence. A second peak in older adults is largely due to Paget disease and prior radiation. In an older patient with known Paget disease, new or worsening localized pain, a growing mass, or a lytic destructive lesion with soft tissue extension suggests sarcoma, which carries a poor prognosis.

blocks.predict: Predict the change in systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output in a patient with Paget disease involving the pelvis, spine, skull, and both femurs.
blocks.explain: Hypervascular bone forms low-resistance arteriovenous channels, so systemic vascular resistance falls and cardiac output rises to keep arterial pressure, which can progress to high-output failure.
blocks.check: Compare the paragraph on high-output heart failure.

blocks.text: Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) is infarction of bone and marrow after its blood supply is interrupted. It occurs where bone is covered largely by articular cartilage and fed by end arteries with little collateral flow, so the subchondral region of a convex joint surface is most vulnerable. The femoral head is the most common site. In adults it depends mainly on retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, which run up the femoral neck beneath the synovial reflection; the artery of the ligament of the head (from the obturator artery) contributes little after childhood. Other sites are the scaphoid, talus, humeral head, and lunate.

Fracture causes AVN by tearing these vessels. A displaced femoral neck fracture is intracapsular and disrupts the retinacular arteries, while an intertrochanteric fracture lies outside the capsule and seldom does. In the scaphoid, branches of the radial artery enter the distal pole and flow backward to the proximal pole, so a waist fracture leaves the proximal pole without supply.

rows: Marrow fat cells enlarge and raise intraosseous pressure; fat emboli; osteocyte apoptosis

Sickled red cells occlude marrow sinusoids
Vasculitis, antiphospholipid thrombosis, and glucocorticoid therapy
Gaucher disease (marrow packing), radiation, hypercoagulable states
blocks.caption: Many nontraumatic cases share the same end point: raised pressure inside a closed marrow cavity or occlusion of its small vessels.

blocks.title: Course of femoral head osteonecrosis
steps: Blood flow to subchondral bone is interrupted
Marrow and osteocytes die; lacunae empty
Living margin becomes hyperemic and fibrotic

Articular surface collapses and flattens
Secondary osteoarthritis develops
blocks.caption: Repair removes dead bone faster than new bone can carry load, which explains collapse months after the infarct.

blocks.text: Dead trabeculae keep their mineral, so radiographs are normal early. MRI is the most sensitive test, showing marrow edema and a double-line sign at the boundary between dead and living bone. Later radiographs show sclerosis, a subchondral lucent crescent, and collapse. Patients have deep groin, buttock, or thigh pain on weight bearing, with limited internal rotation of the hip.

blocks.predict: A 78-year-old woman falls and sustains a displaced femoral neck fracture; her neighbor has an intertrochanteric fracture. Which hip is at greater risk of AVN, and why?
blocks.explain: The femoral neck fracture, because it is intracapsular and tears the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery; the intertrochanteric fracture is extracapsular and leaves them intact.
blocks.check: Compare the paragraph on fracture and femoral head blood supply.

blocks.text: Three childhood hip disorders are separated mainly by age, because each reflects the weakest structure of the hip at that stage of growth. In the newborn it is a shallow socket and a lax capsule, in the young child it is the blood supply of the femoral head epiphysis, and in the adolescent it is the growth plate (physis).

Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) is abnormal development of the acetabulum and femoral head, ranging from a shallow socket to frank dislocation. The acetabulum deepens only when a well-seated femoral head presses into it, so a head that is unstable or out of place leaves the socket shallow. Risk factors are female sex (maternal relaxin and estrogen increase ligament laxity), breech position, first pregnancy, oligohydramnios, and family history. The Barlow test adducts the flexed hip and pushes posteriorly to dislocate an unstable hip; the Ortolani test abducts the hip and lifts the greater trochanter to reduce a dislocated hip with a palpable clunk. Ultrasound is used in early infancy because the femoral head is cartilage until its ossification center appears at about 4 to 6 months. Older infants show limited abduction, a shorter thigh on the affected side (Galeazzi sign), and later a limp. Untreated DDH leads to early osteoarthritis.

Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head epiphysis in children, usually boys about 4 to 8 years old. Between infancy and adolescence the epiphysis depends on a limited retinacular supply, and the growth plate blocks flow from the metaphysis. The child has a painless or mildly painful limp, sometimes with knee pain, and limited abduction and internal rotation. The head then fragments, revascularizes, and remodels; younger children remodel better.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) occurs in obese adolescents during the growth spurt, more often in boys. Shear force fails the physis through its hypertrophic zone, and the femoral neck displaces anteriorly and upward while the epiphysis stays in the acetabulum, so the epiphysis appears to slip posteriorly and medially off the neck (ice cream off a cone). The hip is externally rotated and loses internal rotation, and hip pain may be referred to the knee through the obturator nerve. SCFE in a child outside the usual age range or in a thin child suggests hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency or therapy, or renal osteodystrophy. Unstable slips can cause AVN.

blocks.title: Pediatric hip disorders compared
blocks.caption: Hip disease often presents as knee pain in children, so the hip must be examined in any limping child.

blocks.text: Each intervertebral disc has a central nucleus pulposus, a notochord-derived gel of proteoglycan, water, and type II collagen, surrounded by the annulus fibrosus, concentric lamellae of fibrocartilage with type I collagen in the outer rings. The nucleus converts axial load into hoop tension in the annulus. With age the nucleus loses proteoglycan and water, the disc loses height, and the annulus develops fissures. A sudden or repetitive load, often flexion with rotation, can then push nucleus material through an annular tear.

Herniations are usually posterolateral, because the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and reinforces only the midline. Most lumbar herniations occur at L4 to L5 or L5 to S1, where load and motion are greatest. Each lumbar root exits the foramen beneath the pedicle of its own vertebra, above the level of the disc below. A posterolateral L4 to L5 herniation therefore misses the exiting L4 root and compresses the L5 root as it descends toward its foramen. A far lateral herniation into the foramen compresses the exiting root instead (L4). In the cervical spine, roots exit above their own vertebra, so the C5 to C6 disc also affects the lower-numbered root, C6. Pain arises from compression and from inflammation provoked by extruded nucleus material, and the outer annulus itself is innervated. A large central herniation can compress the cauda equina, causing saddle anesthesia and urinary retention.

blocks.title: Localizing a lumbar herniation
blocks.text: A 42-year-old man has back pain radiating down the lateral leg to the top of the foot, weak great toe extension, and normal knee and ankle reflexes. Step 1: the sensory and motor pattern matches L5. Step 2: normal patellar (L4) and Achilles (S1) reflexes fit, because L5 has no reliable reflex. Step 3: a posterolateral herniation compresses the traversing root, which is the lower root of the pair, so the disc is L4 to L5. Step 4: if imaging instead showed a far lateral L4 to L5 herniation, the exiting L4 root would be affected and the patellar reflex would fall.

Growing adolescents have two vulnerable structures at the knee: apophyses, which are cartilage-rich secondary ossification centers at tendon attachments, and the articular cartilage and subchondral bone of the joint surfaces. Rapid growth tightens muscles and tendons, and sports add repeated load, so these structures fail under traction or shear.

Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle. Repeated quadriceps contraction during running and jumping pulls through the patellar ligament on the immature tubercle and produces small avulsions with reactive new bone. Athletic adolescents, often around 10 to 15 years old during the growth spurt, have pain and a tender bony prominence below the patella that is worse with kneeling, jumping, and stairs. It resolves when the apophysis fuses, sometimes leaving a permanent bump or a separate ossicle.

Chondromalacia patellae is softening and fibrillation of the articular cartilage on the back of the patella, usually in adolescents and young adults, more often female. Abnormal patellar tracking and repetitive patellofemoral loading concentrate stress on the cartilage. Anterior knee pain worsens with stairs, squatting, and prolonged sitting with the knees flexed, when patellofemoral pressure is high, and crepitus may be felt. Its cartilage breakdown resembles early osteoarthritis but is localized to the patella and occurs in the young.

Osteochondritis dissecans is separation of a fragment of subchondral bone with its overlying cartilage, most often from the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle. Repetitive microtrauma and a fragile subchondral blood supply are the leading explanations. A stable fragment causes activity-related pain and effusion; a detached fragment becomes a loose body that causes catching or locking. Lesions in children with open physes heal more readily than those in adults.

blocks.text: Dupuytren contracture is a superficial fibromatosis of the palmar aponeurosis, the dense fascial sheet that lies under the palmar skin, superficial to the flexor tendons. Fibroblasts in the fascia differentiate into myofibroblasts, which contain alpha smooth muscle actin, contract like smooth muscle, and secrete collagen, initially type III. Transforming growth factor beta drives this differentiation. Proliferating myofibroblasts first form firm nodules in the palm, then longitudinal cords along the fascial bands. As the cords contract and are stabilized by new collagen, they shorten and pull the fingers into flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and then the proximal interphalangeal joints.

The ring finger is most often affected, followed by the little finger, and both hands are often involved. The contracture is usually painless, although early nodules may be tender. Because the flexor tendons themselves are normal, the finger cannot be fully extended passively or actively, and the patient cannot lay the palm flat on a table. Cords can also displace the digital neurovascular bundles.

Risk is highest in men over about 50 of northern European ancestry, with a family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance of variable penetrance. Diabetes mellitus, heavy alcohol use, smoking, and epilepsy are associated. The same myofibroblast process in other sites produces plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease) and penile fibromatosis (Peyronie disease), which may coexist with Dupuytren contracture.

integration.text: Osteoporosis and Paget disease are both disorders of remodeling, and the coupling of osteoclasts to osteoblasts predicts their labs when they are set beside osteomalacia. In osteoporosis, resorption slightly exceeds formation but both are within normal limits, so ALP is normal. In Paget disease, both are greatly increased and remain coupled, so ALP rises while calcium stays normal. In osteomalacia, osteoid is made but not mineralized, so ALP and PTH rise, phosphate falls, and calcium is low or low normal. Avascular necrosis adds anatomy: the same retinacular arteries explain why femoral neck fractures, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, and unstable SCFE all threaten the femoral head, while sickle cell disease, lupus, and decompression sickness reach bone through the circulation.

Cartilage, disc, and fascia fail through matrix biology. Osteoarthritis and disc degeneration both begin with proteoglycan and water loss that removes a tissue's ability to bear load, and both later cause osteophytes that can narrow joints and foramina. Clinical correlation has limits: radiographic OA and MRI disc bulges are common in people without symptoms, so a finding must match the patient's pain pattern and neurologic signs before it explains them.

summary: Osteoarthritis is mechanical cartilage failure: catabolic chondrocytes degrade aggrecan and type II collagen, and bone responds with sclerosis, eburnation, cysts, and osteophytes.
Osteoarthritis causes use-related pain, stiffness under 30 minutes, DIP and PIP bony nodes, normal labs, and uneven joint space narrowing without erosions.
Osteoporosis is less bone of normal composition; estrogen loss raises RANKL and lowers osteoprotegerin, and trabecular bone thins first.
Osteoporosis labs are normal; DEXA T-score of minus 2.5 or lower defines osteoporosis, and minus 1 to minus 2.5 defines osteopenia.
Paget disease starts with giant hyperactive osteoclasts, ends with thick, weak mosaic bone, and shows an isolated high ALP.
Paget complications follow from enlarged, weak, hypervascular bone: nerve compression, hearing loss, fractures, high-output heart failure, and osteosarcoma.
Avascular necrosis is bone infarction in end-arterial subchondral bone; the femoral head, fed by the medial circumflex femoral artery, is most common, and MRI detects it first.
Age separates pediatric hip disorders: DDH in newborns, Legg-Calve-Perthes at about 4 to 8 years, SCFE in obese adolescents.
Posterolateral lumbar disc herniation compresses the traversing lower root, so L4 to L5 affects L5.
Osgood-Schlatter is tibial tubercle traction apophysitis; Dupuytren contracture is myofibroblast shortening of palmar fascia that flexes the ring and little fingers.
